citation: Oka (2025), “Evaluating Large Language Models on the Frame and Symbol Grounding Problems: A Zero-shot Benchmark”
evidence: Operationalizes the frame problem as relevance filtering and plan revision, and symbol grounding as integrating a novel object into coherent meanings; evaluates 13 models with repeated trials and criteria for contextual reasoning, semantic coherence, information filtering, and consistency. Source: https://arxiv.org/html/2506.07896v1

citation: Galatolo, Rappuoli, Winkle & Beloucif (2025), “Beyond Ethical Alignment: Evaluating LLMs as Artificial Moral Assistants”
evidence: Defines Artificial Moral Assistant reasoning and evaluates deductive and abductive moral reasoning chains plus chain assessment, rather than only final ethical verdict agreement. Source: https://arxiv.org/html/2508.12754v1

citation: Wang & Song (2024/2025), “MARS: Benchmarking the Metaphysical Reasoning Abilities of Language Models with a Multi-task Evaluation Dataset”
evidence: Introduces three discriminative tasks for plausibility of action changes, resulting state changes, and situational transitions; evaluates 20 language models. The staged labels expose intermediate metaphysical reasoning failures. Source: https://arxiv.org/html/2406.02106v2

citation: Wang et al. (2026), “A Philosophy-Grounded Approach to Assessing LLM-Clinical Medical Ethics Alignment”
evidence: Introduces 3,648 expert-validated questions grounded in principlism: 2,182 knowledge MCQs and 1,466 open-ended clinical dilemmas requiring explicit multi-principle trade-off reasoning. Source: https://aclanthology.org/2026.findings-acl.1806.pdf

citation: Cooper, Oesterheld, Nguyen, Kastner & Perez (2026), “A dataset of rated conceptual arguments”
evidence: Provides 951 critiques of 442 position texts, including normative ethics and philosophy of mind, with 1,458 expert ratings for centrality, strength, correctness, clarity, dead weight, single-issue focus, and overall quality; supports argument-level evaluation when bottom-line philosophical truth is unavailable. Source: https://arxiv.org/html/2607.27499v1

citation: Yang et al. (2025), “InterIDEAS: Philosophical Intertextuality via LLMs”
evidence: Combines authentic philosophical texts, bibliometric relations, retrieval-augmented generation, LLM extraction, and human-in-the-loop validation; releases 2,236 reference–attitude pairs for evaluating grounded philosophical-text relation extraction and analysis. Source: https://aclanthology.org/2025.emnlp-main.1180/

citation: Asghari & Biały (2025), “Triangles, Justice, and AI: Testing Large Language Models’ Comprehension of Political Ideologies”
benchmark_type: philosophical theory application and reflection evaluation
evidence: Tests seven models on recall, application, and reflection for Rawlsian and Nozickian theories in a controlled novel scenario; the staged rubric distinguishes memorization from theory transfer and reflective reasoning. Source: https://journals.ub.uni-koeln.de/index.php/phidi/article/view/11663

citation: Wu et al. (2023), “Hence, Socrates is mortal: A Benchmark for Natural Language Syllogistic Reasoning”
evidence: Covers a taxonomy of categorical syllogisms with template-generated items, GPT-3 paraphrases, and 1,000 manually rewritten test examples; provides generation and multiple-choice validity labels. Source: https://aclanthology.org/2023.findings-acl.148/

citation: Han et al. (2022/2024), “FOLIO: Natural Language Reasoning with First-Order Logic”
evidence: Contains 1,430 conclusions over 487 human-authored premise sets with first-order-logic annotations and executable verification; separates natural-language deduction from NL-to-FOL formalization. Included as a formal reasoning control, not as philosophy-domain content. Source: https://arxiv.org/abs/2209.00840

citation: Ruiz-Dolz, Kikteva & Lawrence (2025), “Mining Complex Patterns of Argumentative Reasoning in Natural Language Dialogue”
evidence: Introduces 441 dialogue arguments annotated with 24 argumentation schemes and evaluates scheme mining; labels expose premise/conclusion or inference-form structure useful for inspectable philosophical argument evaluation. Source: https://aclanthology.org/2025.acl-long.368/

citation: Bezou-Vrakatseli, Cocarascu & Modgil (2025), “Can Large Language Models Understand Argument Schemes?”
evidence: Evaluates seven LLMs on manually annotated and generated enthymemes under zero-shot, few-shot, and chain-of-thought conditions; the labels expose argument form rather than only final answer preference. Source: https://aclanthology.org/2025.findings-acl.702/
